articles.title: Lyle Odelein Dies at Age 58, Blue Jackets' 1st Captain Won NHL Stanley Cup in 1993
articles.summary: Former NHL defenseman Lyle Odelein died Friday at the age of 58, the league announced.
articles.body:
Former NHL defenseman Lyle Odelein died Friday at the age of 58, the league announced .

Odelein spent 16 seasons in the NHL and suited up for eight teams, including the Montreal Canadiens, New Jersey Devils, Phoenix Coyotes, Columbus Blue Jackets, Chicago Blackhawks, Dallas Stars, Florida Panthers and Pittsburgh Penguins. He won the 1993 Stanley Cup with the Canadiens before becoming the first captain in Blue Jackets franchise history.

In 1,056 NHL games, Odelein scored 252 points (50 goals, 202 assists) and racked up 2,316 penalty minutes, which ranks 30th in league history. He played in 86 career playoff games and scored 18 points (five goals, 13 assists).

The NHL noted that Odelein "valiantly battled myriad, life-threatening health issues eight years ago, undergoing the replacement of his heart's aortic valve and receiving a new liver and kidneys in a marathon surgical procedure on April 4, 2018, in Pittsburgh." He managed to take part in the special Bell Centre ceremony on Oct. 11, 2018, where the Canadiens celebrated their 1993 Stanley Cup title.

"I grew up in Saskatchewan as a Canadiens fan, so playing there for six and a half years was … wow!" Odelein told reporters at the ceremony. "It was so special. The French people treated me like a god. I can't say enough about Montreal. It is by far my favorite city, best memories in the world. For me to be there (at the ceremony) is just awesome. I just want to say thank you so much to the fans and God bless. Everybody in Montreal treated me like a king. I don't even know what to say. Montreal was my city. It was phenomenal. I feel basically so blessed that I've been given a new life. It's great."

articles.body: NEW DELHI: India's wrestlers arrived in Aichi-Nagoya carrying questions over injuries, form and confidence. They left with six medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze — and a much bigger target already occupying their minds: the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal struck gold, while Nitesh Siwach and Antim Panghal won silver and Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar added bronze.The campaign was also marked by two major statements. Sehrawat defeated reigning world champion Han Chong Song in the men's 57kg freestyle final, while Kalkal beat Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka on his way to gold in the 65kg category.For the Indian wrestlers, however, Nagoya was less about looking back at what they had achieved and more about building towards what comes next.Sehrawat turns a difficult phase into goldFor Sehrawat, the gold was the culmination of one of the most difficult phases of his young career.The 23-year-old had won bronze at the Paris Olympics but subsequently struggled with motivation in 2025. A persistent stomach ailment also forced him to miss important competitions.In Nagoya, however, Sehrawat rediscovered his best. He defeated reigning world champion Han Chong Song 11-7 in the final, recovering after the North Korean had turned a 1-6 deficit into a 7-6 lead.It was Sehrawat's first Asian Games gold after his bronze at Hangzhou."Ups and downs, injuries keep happening like this. That phase also comes, but I had the belief in my mind. We should never give up, and I did the same. Today, I have won a gold medal in the Games. The future goal is the Olympics," Sehrawat said after returning to India.He said the next goal was to replicate the achievement on the biggest stage."We won gold for the country. The plan for the future is exactly the same — we will win gold for the country and prepare accordingly. I thank all the countrymen; it was their prayers that worked in the matches," he added.Then came the statement that perhaps best captured the mood of India's wrestling contingent."...now we will do better in the future. The whole nation is giving us love. Now our national anthem will be played at the LA Olympics."Kalkal follows gold with an Olympic-sized ambitionIf Sehrawat's gold was a comeback story, Kalkal's was a lesson in refusing to surrender.The world No. 2 entered the Asian Games unbeaten this season and lived up to his billing in the men's 65kg freestyle category.Before the final, Kalkal defeated Japan's Olympic champion Kiyooka and Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi. Against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final, he appeared to be heading towards defeat after falling 2-9 behind.Instead, he produced a stunning late comeback to win 10-9.The victory restored India's hold on the 65kg Asian Games title, a category in which Yogeshwar Dutt and Bajrang Punia had previously won gold."Whatever struggle I did has paid off. The final match was tough, but I was only thinking of winning that time," Kalkal said.His sights are already firmly fixed on Los Angeles."Now we will practice more, and if all goes well, we will win gold at the Olympics too. For the Olympics, the practice has already begun," Kalkal added.From selling milk to a historic Greco-Roman finalNitesh Siwach's silver carried perhaps the most remarkable backstory of India's six medallists.A serious knee injury as a teenager kept him away from wrestling for more than 18 months. During that period, he helped his family with its dairy business and sold milk in Panipat.His comeback culminated in an historic Asian Games final appearance in the men's 97kg Greco-Roman category — India's first in the weight class in 64 years.Siwach eventually lost 0-4 to Japan's Yuri Nakazato but returned home with a silver medal and a clear Olympic target."I feel great. This is the first time I am getting such respect and honour. I am experiencing such a great welcome for the first time, and I am very happy," he said. "I had aimed for gold. I didn't win gold, but I did secure the silver medal and I am very happy about that. Since this was my first Asian Games, I am delighted with the silver."Siwach also believes India's Greco-Roman wrestlers can make their presence felt in Los Angeles."People used to say we wouldn't win medals in Greco-Roman, but we will continue to excel. We will bring home medals from the Los Angeles Olympics," he said.His personal target is even clearer."I made some mistakes, which is why I had to settle for silver. My goal going forward is to win gold at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and I will work extremely hard for it," he added.He has already begun that preparation."My preparation for the Olympics has already begun, starting from the very day I won the medal. I have to bring a gold in the Olympics," Siwach said.Punia battles through a new weight categoryDeepak Punia's bronze was another product of perseverance.The 2019 World Championships silver medallist had competed at 86kg and 92kg before moving to 97kg this year following a muscle injury.Despite the challenges of changing weight categories, Punia earned selection for the Asian Games and defeated Mongolia's Gankhuyag Ganbaatar 2-1 in the bronze-medal bout."Winning a medal was quite challenging for me because I used to compete in the 86kg category, but this time I participated in the 97kg category. There were many challenges, and my hope and goal was to win the gold medal. However, I had to settle for the bronze," Punia said.Experience helped him deal with the pressure."I have been playing for a long time, so there is pressure; there is pressure on every athlete. But I understood how I had to handle the pressure. In my mind, it was just that I had to give my best. It was not like I had to take over-pressure. I just had to give my 100 per cent and that's what I did," he said.Panghal improves on Hangzhou, Kumar makes historyAntim Panghal also upgraded her medal from bronze at Hangzhou to silver in the women's 53kg category.She lost 1-9 to Japan's Moe Kiyooka in the final after coaches had worked on keeping her calm and confident before the competition."It is my second time winning a medal. But I had thought that I had to come first, but I could not come first. In the future, I will try to do better than this," Panghal said.Sunil Kumar, meanwhile, returned to the podium after knee surgery to win bronze in the men's 87kg Greco-Roman category. He defeated the Philippines' Callum Johnston Roberts 9-0 by technical superiority, becoming the first Indian Greco-Roman wrestler to win two Asian Games medals after his bronze at Hangzhou."I am very happy and want to thank all my fellow countrymen. May your blessings and support continue to be with me," Kumar said.Six medals, one bigger dreamThe six medals tell only part of India’s wrestling story in Nagoya.Sehrawat battled through a difficult phase to defeat a reigning world champion. Kalkal stunned an Olympic champion before producing a remarkable comeback for gold. Siwach overcame a serious teenage injury and years of struggle to reach a historic Greco-Roman final. Punia changed weight categories and still made the podium, while Panghal improved her medal colour and Kumar returned from knee surgery to make history.But beyond the six medals was a bigger message — India’s wrestlers are already looking towards Los Angeles.Their words after returning home reflected an ambition that goes far beyond Nagoya: to turn this success into Olympic gold in 2028.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: “There aren’t really that many schools”: How Naomi Osaka turned her father’s Haitian roots into a family mission to help children, years before her tennis fame
articles.summary: Naomi Osaka’s connection to Haiti began long before she became a Grand Slam champion.
articles.body: Naomi Osaka’s connection to Haiti began long before she became a Grand Slam champion. Her father, Leonard “Maxime” Francois, returned to his hometown of Jacmel and started the Osaka Foundation with her mother, Tamaki Osaka, in 1999. The family built an education and sports centre for children in the community, creating a project that existed years before Naomi became a global tennis star.For Naomi, the foundation became more personal when she finally visited Haiti. Her first trip came in Oct. 2017. She returned in November 2018, just two months after winning her first Grand Slam title at the US Open.Naomi Osaka saw her father’s legacy firsthand in HaitiThe Osaka Foundation began after Francois returned to Jacmel, where he wanted to help children in his community. The foundation says the family set aside 20 acres for the project and initially focused on tennis. It later developed into a centre built around both sport and education. Children receive access to schooling, food, housing and sports opportunities.Naomi had never visited Haiti before 2017. During her first trip, she visited her father’s hometown and met children connected to the family’s work.“I wanted to visit Haiti,” Osaka said about her first trip, explaining that she wanted to see her father’s homeland herself despite hearing negative comments about the country. She later said, “Haiti is a beautiful little country,” after experiencing the country firsthand.Her connection grew stronger during her Nov. 2018 return. By then, Osaka had become one of tennis’ biggest names after beating Serena Williams in the US Open final in Sept. 2018.The Miami Herald reported in March 2019 that the highlight of Osaka’s trip was visiting the IOA Center, the elementary school her parents had helped build in Jacmel. The family continued to provide funding, uniforms and supplies, while the school also unveiled a new wing during her visit.Naomi Osaka's tennis success helped extend the family’s workOsaka later used one of her new commercial opportunities to support the centre. In March 2019, after becoming part of Barbie’s Sheroes collection, she said she would donate her Barbie partnership fee to the IOA Center.“I think that it’s really important because, especially in Haiti, there aren’t really that many schools,” Osaka said at Indian Wells in March 2019 while discussing the donation. She said the money would help expand the centre, with tennis courts also under consideration.That donation connected Osaka’s growing career directly to the project her parents had started two decades earlier.Her Haiti work later expanded beyond the family foundation. In Aug. 2021, after a 7.2-magnitude earthquake struck Haiti, Osaka pledged her prize money from the Western & Southern Open to earthquake relief. She made the announcement before the tournament and said the devastation in her father’s country deeply affected her.The same personal connection also shaped her Play Academy work. In 2021, the program expanded to Haiti, where it partnered with local sports organisations to create more opportunities for girls.For Osaka, Haiti has remained tied to family, sport and the community her father chose to support. articles.title: Warriors' Steph Curry has concerning bench routine as injury concerns linger from last season
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors superstar has been vocal about his knee injury and that he is fine heading into the season. For now he might be, but his new routine on...
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors have had all eyes on Steph Curry throughout the offseason for various reasons, but the biggest one might just be whether he was going to stay or not. Both sides finally agreed on a contract extension.

The Warriors are going to be an interesting team to watch this season. Curry also has a lingering knee injury.

"There's at least some lingering concern about the knee. From what I've been told, it can be managed, but it has to be managed and that's a new thing for Steph because people always say he is the most conditioned guy in the League and now he has to manage a knee. I guess we'll find out, but from what I understand, he and his trainers have devised ways to kind of work around that and sort of support that whole possibility of the knee not being as great as he wants it to be. So, I'm curious to see how it turns out, but Steph seemed pretty confident that he'll be able to go out there and put out 70+ games," NBC Sports' Marcus Poole said.

Despite all of the worry from everyone, the four-time NBA champion claims his knee is good.

"Knee's feeling great. Ready to go. No issues. I feel a lot stronger and understanding of what I'm dealing with," Curry said.

Curry has been vocal about having to do different things for treatment this season. One of the new things is keeping a heating pad on his knee when he isn't playing during the game.

"Steph keeps a heating pad on that right knee all the time now whenever he's not in the game," The Athletic's Nick Friedell wrote.

This is something new for Curry, but it keeps the concerning status of that knee around as he is having to do extra things to keep it healthy. If he isn't on top of it, he has already mentioned that it could cost him some games.

The upcoming season is going to be a learning curve for the former MVP and fans as they watch him navigate the lingering issue. Curry is going to play unless he absolutely can't, but with him having to do all of this, it is worth keeping an eye on.

articles.title: The Travis Hunter 2-way Jaguars experience appears to be totally dead
articles.summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars took care of business once again in Week 4. Jacksonville held off Cincinnati in a 22-17 win and improved to 3-1 on the season. As th...
articles.body:
The Jacksonville Jaguars took care of business once again in Week 4. Jacksonville held off Cincinnati in a 22-17 win and improved to 3-1 on the season. As the 2026 season progresses, it is becoming abundantly clear which position the Jaguars prefer to play Travis Hunter in during his sophomore campaign.

Jacksonville's two-way star was billed as both a cornerback and wide receiver coming out of the draft. But he appears to almost exclusively play cornerback during his time in the NFL.

In fact, every single snap that Hunter played against the Bengals was on the defensive side of the ball. Yes, 100% of Hunter's 76 snaps came at cornerback and none at the wide receiver position.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Hunter did split some time between offense and defense as a rookie. He moonlighted on the offensive side, logging 28 receptions for 298 receiving yards and a touchdown through seven games. At the same time, he put up solid defensive production too. However, all of that has changed during the first four games of this season.

Hunter only has one reception for eight yards and one carry for three yards on the offensive side of the ball in 2026. Meanwhile, he's been getting almost all of his reps on defense. That was especially surprising in Week 4 after Cincinnati lost Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins to injuries. If there was ever a time to sprinkle Hunter in on offense, that was it.

The clues were there starting in Week 1. During the season opener, Hunter only played 7% of offensive snaps .

Jaguars fans should not get their hopes up about anything changing anytime soon. Head coach Liam Coen declared that he doesn't care where Hunter was draft , he just wants to win football games. If Jacksonville's coaching staff doesn't care about getting less out of Hunter then this could simply be the new normal for him.

Either way, the Jaguars are winning games this season. They are 3-1 and in sole possession of first place in the AFC South division standings.

Next up for Jacksonville is a Week 5 matchup against the Eagles.

articles.title: 112 yards later, the Giants finally have their No. 1 receiver back
articles.summary: Six catches. 112 yards. His first touchdown of the season. Malik Nabers gave the Giants the kind of receiving performance […]
articles.body:
Six catches. 112 yards. His first touchdown of the season. Malik Nabers gave the Giants the kind of receiving performance they have been waiting for in Sunday's 36-24 win over Arizona.

The touchdown was especially important. Arvell Reese's third-quarter interception gave New York the ball at the Cardinals' 26, and Jameis Winston found Nabers for a 25-yard score. It turned a defensive takeaway into a lead. Nabers also made a 39-yard catch on third down earlier in the game, winning a jump ball that kept another drive alive.

Giants need Nabers as more than a target count

When Nabers gets the ball downfield, the offense looks different. A six-catch day can be ordinary for a receiver with his role; 112 yards and two chunk plays are not. Those plays change how a defense can handle the rest of the lineup, especially on the downs when New York has to throw.

Winston spread the ball around Sunday. Isaiah Likely caught seven passes for 66 yards, and Theo Johnson scored on his only target. The offense works better when Nabers can command attention without being the only option. The Giants can still make their top receiver the player opponents have to account for first without treating everyone else as an afterthought.

I would be careful about declaring the offense fixed after one afternoon. New York scored 36 points, but the final six came on Deonte Banks' interception return. The real encouragement is more specific: Nabers created yards and finished a scoring chance, two things the Giants cannot afford to leave out of their passing game.

New York has also found early reliability from Isaiah Likely . If opponents start leaning coverage toward Nabers again, that second option should get useful chances. If they do not, the Giants should keep testing them deep.

articles.title: Jalen Brunson’s first Knicks minutes since wrist surgery are almost here
articles.summary: The last time Jalen Brunson played against another NBA team, he scored 45 points to close out the Finals. On […]
articles.body:
The last time Jalen Brunson played against another NBA team, he scored 45 points to close out the Finals. On Monday, he is expected to get a much shorter shift when the Knicks open preseason play against Philadelphia.

The limited stint makes sense. Brunson underwent left wrist surgery in July and said in late September that he had been fully cleared. Coach Mike Brown has said his starters will play in the opener, but not much. The Knicks do not need a preseason scoring display from their captain. They need to see him move, handle the ball and leave the game healthy.

Knicks have time to build Brunson back up

Brunson averaged 26.0 points and 6.8 assists last season. His 45-point Game 5 against San Antonio brought New York its first title since 1973 and the Finals MVP award. None of that makes Monday's exhibition meaningless, but it does put the priorities in order. A few clean possessions after surgery are a better result than 25 hard minutes in early October.

The useful part of a limited stint will be watching how Brunson and the other starters share the floor under Brown. New York has spent camp sorting out its depth, including a fight for the final roster place . The starting group does not need an overhaul, but its timing has to return before the games count.

I would pay more attention to Brunson's comfort catching and passing with his left hand than to his point total. He says he is cleared. This is the first public chance to see what that looks like against defenders, with no reason to ask him to play through discomfort for an exhibition result.

The Knicks open the regular season later this month. If Monday gives Brunson an uneventful first run and Brown a chance to test the lineup, the short night will have done its job.

Bradford City are expected to name Michael Duff as the new manager according to reports.

The Bantams have been looking for a new boss after Graham Alexander left the club to join Championship side Preston North End last week.

According to journalists Jamie Raynor and Ian Woodcock of BBC Sport , former Northern Ireland international defender Duff will take over.

Former Cheltenham Town and Swansea City manager Duff helped Wycombe Wanderers to an 11th-placed finish in League One last campaign but was sacked by the club after seven winless games earlier this season. In total, Duff 52 games as Wycombe boss, winning 20, drawing 15, and suffering 17 defeats.

Whilst some players see international breaks merely as matches that add to an already packed schedule, others consider them an opportunity to gain the playing time with the national team that they are missing out on at club level. Such is certainly the case for Mika Godts (21).

Set to make his fourth consecutive start for Belgium against France this Monday, the Parisian winger has used the past few weeks to get back into the rhythm of competitive football. Because since his arrival at Paris Saint-Germain this summer, it's hard to say that the former Ajax player has really been able to get a proper taste of it.

Having made six appearances (144 minutes of playing time) for his new club since the start of the season, Godts has so far been confined to a role as an exclusive substitute. But that's no reason to dampen the Belgian's ambitions; he sees himself following in the footsteps of his team-mate Désiré Doué (21).

"I need time," he explained to the press on the sidelines of the match against Les Bleus . "I've only just arrived in Paris. It's a very, very big club. I'm staying calm. I'm trying to learn from the best, to show plenty of confidence, and to give my very best. I know I'll reach his level."

articles.title: Florida HS football recruiting: We saw a few elite prospects up close
articles.summary: Florida's biggest football powerhouses had a big slate of games in Week 7. USA TODAY was on the sidelines as marquee recruits shined.
articles.body:
Week 7 in Florida gave us some elite matchups, and they lived up to the hype.

South Florida powerhouses St. Thomas Aquinas and Chaminade-Madonna faced off in a classic in Hollywood on Friday, Oct. 3, and IMG Academy hosted The St. James Performance Academy, which announced its arrival to the national stage by pushing the Ascenders to the brink at home.

USA TODAY's Florida network was on hand for both heavyweight bouts, and the stars shined for Florida's premier football talent factories.

Here are recruiting takeaways from a heavy-duty weekend of high school football in Florida:

Osani Gayles is as good as better than advertised

With Eric McFarland III and Eric Whitfield out for IMG, Gayles rose to the task. He was the No. 1 option fin the win, catching nine passes for 185 yards and two touchdowns . He had a 63-yard catch that up a touchdown in the fourth quarter, and his 73-yard kick return that put the Scenders in range for the game-winning field goal.

Gayles is the No. 13 overall player in the USA TODAY Florida Top 100 midseason update. He's devastating in the open field, and he looked uncatchable against the Strivers. It was a fitting night for the Alabama commit, who watched the Tide pour 56 points on a ranked Mississippi State a few hours before stuffing the stat sheet himself.

"It's fun to watch (Alabama's) offense," Gayles said. "Just seeing Lotzier (Brooks), Rico (Scott), Ryan (Coleman-Williams) do their things, so it's good to see that I could possibly be one of them. And then obviously Keelon (Russell) keeps progressing as a quarterback and being able to throw the ball downfield. I feel like he's getting better every game. It's exciting to see."

Censere Gaylord is not talked about enough

Gaylord is ranked as the No. 16 player in Florida and No. 2 cornerback, but he just isn't talked about as much as other defensive backs in the state. Part of it is because he just quietly shuts down his side of the field in Bradenton.

Gaylord swung the game twice in the win over TSJPA. His first pick came in the third quarter with the Strivers driving and poised to take a two-score lead. His one-handed tip-drill pick quelled the drive and set up an IMG touchdown on the ensuing possession. His second pick ended as a 97-yard pick-six that broke a 28-28 tie.

The Huskie commit reaffirmed his commitment to Washington, confirming again that his recruitment is shut down and his only gameday visit in the works is back to Seattle.

Ohio State got a good one in Wyatt Smith

St. Thomas Aquinas has spent most of the year as the No. 1 team in the nation , and there is an argument that no single Raider has had more of an impact on their success than Smith.

The Buckeye commit and No. 10 player in Florida stepped up when it mattered most against cross-town rivals Chaminade-Madonna. On top of registering a sack, Smith blocked the Lions' look at a go-ahead field goal in the fourth quarter , and was credited with 13 tackles and four pass breakups at the line of scrimmage.

Elite programs still pushing for 5-star OT Mark Matthews

Matthews was a sturdy presence up front for a shaky Raider offense, and even played interior defensive lineman alongside Smith on a few key situations against Chaminade-Madonna.

He has been committed to Texas A&M since the spring , and has stayed tethered despite pushed from big-name coaching staffs that have been in the hunt for years. For now, it's the relationships that have kept Matthews with an impressively stacked Aggie class.

"I guess you could say it's how I built a family with the players that are already over there," Matthews said. "That was my main point, that I built a good family with them. So I felt comfortable with those guys that I'm going to be living with and hanging out with."

That doesn't other programs have given up. While Matthews says "everyone" is still calling, there are programs that are stronger flip candidates than most.

Miami has long been attached to the star tackle, and he confirmed the 'Canes are still in pursuit. Keep an eye on LSU as well. Lane Kiffin has never been shy of taking big recruiting swings, and Matthews said the Tigers are a realistic school still pushing.

Let's start with the receiver core, which features Tromon Isaac Jr. and Armani Strong. Isaac was electric against an elite Raider secondary, and finished the night with six catches for 145 yards and one touchdown — which was an impressive one-handed snag in coverage in the back of the end zone.

Strong, a Florida commit , was effective as a release valve for the Lions, catching six passes for 44 yards, but just as importantly forced the Raiders to pick their poison in coverage.

Peter Pierre is one of the most intriguing prospects in his class. The 6-foot-5, 220-pound athlete caught five passes for 49 yards, but is also an eye-catching prospect as a pass rusher. He has elite speed and hands for his size, good strength, and continues to look more polished week-over-week.

Pierre, Strong and Isaac all recently went on a visit to Gainesville together for Florida's statement win over Ole Miss.

Brady Quinn was surgical in the loss, tossing for 263 yards on 19-of-25 completions with one touchdown pass and one interception. Quinn was a true signal caller on the final driver, leading Chaminade-Madonna down the field on quick, accurate passes to the boundary while making the right reads and checks. He was also dominant on the ground, taking eight carries for 88 yards and two more scores.

Linebacker Karen Holcombe was an unsolvable problem for the Raiders. He was in the backfield all night, registering five tackles for loss while helping stifle a typically lethal Raider ground game.

Is Jayden Wade the No. 1 player in the class 2028?

The 2028 class is really, really elite at the national level. Florida players make up a significant portion of the rankings. Wade was initially the No. 1 overall player in the country when 247Sports put out its initial 2028 rankings, and he currently sits at the No. 8 spot nationally.

If he keeps up this pace, it'll be the lowest his ranking sits until signing day.

All the Georgia commit has done this season is make defenses look silly. He's only needed the first half in all but two games to put games away. Against TSJPA, he tossed for 348 yards on 16-of-22 completions with three touchdown passes. He added 39 yards and another score on 15 carries.

Now seven weeks through the season, Wade has thrown for 1,188 yards, and 16 touchdowns on 82 passing attempts with zero interceptions.

He's poised like a second-year college player, and he commands the offense at a cerebral level. He accuracy and timing in the pocket and on the run are truly best-in-class, and he takes full advantage of his loaded receiver core.

articles.title: Two recently extended Steelers defenders must step up now
articles.summary: Nick Herbig and Keanu Benton got paid, but their lack of sack production is hurting T.J. Watt and Pittsburgh's defense through four games.
articles.body:
While media scrutiny following the Pittsburgh Steelers 2–2 start has naturally gravitated toward offensive scheme disconnects and veteran stars like T.J. Watt and Cameron Heyward, a pressing concern resides with the next generation of Pittsburgh's core.

As Christopher Carter reminded fans on his " Locked on Steelers " podcast, defensive tackle Keeanu Benton and edge rusher Nick Herbig, both Wisconsin products and close friends off the field, were rewarded with lucrative, high-priced contract extensions this past offseason. Yet through four games, their lack of game-altering production is quickly becoming a primary bottleneck for a defense hovering around the middle of the NFL pack.

"There's some guys that they've been paid," stated Carter. "They're younger and they need to start producing and producing really, really soon. I'm going to start with one guy, well two guys really, same college. They're best their best buddies. But Nick Herbing and Keeanu Benton right at the top of the list for guys that need to step up and step up now."

The raw statistics tell a stark story for two pass rushers tasked with capitalizing when teams focus their protection schemes on Watt and Heyward.

"Keeanu Benton right now, six pressures, no sacks to start the season right now. And that's a problem. Nick Herbig has four pressures. He's averaging one pressure per game. And you can't say it's just his snap count isn't high enough anymore because it is. And he hasn't registered a sack yet this season."

In addition to going sackless, Herbig missed two tackles in Pittsburgh's recent loss to Cleveland.

When general managers extend young contributors early, they are paying for high-ceiling playmaking, not passive rotation snaps. If Pittsburgh expects to navigate a grueling AFC slate, Benton and Herbig must quickly justify their contract extensions by turning pressures into sacks.

articles.title: Lack of great players causes doubt over Jürgen Klopp’s ability to fix Germany
articles.summary: Can Germany return to its glory days?
articles.body:
Alan Shearer has already set the bar extremely high for Jürgen Klopp — and he is not convinced Germany currently has the talent to reach it.

The former England striker believes Klopp's biggest challenge will be restoring Germany to the powerhouse status the country once enjoyed, arguing that the national team is going through a period where its talent pool simply is not at the level needed to compete consistently for major trophies.

"The big question Klopp has to answer taking over as Germany manager is can he bring them back to being a powerhouse in international football because he's coming at a time where German football isn't at its best. We've seen Germany now in the last few years and I covered them a couple of times in the World Cup and they were really poor," Shearer told Betfair . "I don't think they're blessed with great players. They've got one or two very, very good players, but I think in terms of the numbers, I'd be surprised if he was to get them back to the top level in competing for EUROs and for World Cups. I don't see that happening for a while because I don't think that they have the talent at the minute for them to achieve that, despite how great he is as a manager."

Germany clearly possesses high-end talent in players such as Florian Wirtz and Jamal Musiala, while a number of younger players are now breaking into the senior setup. But Shearer believes the overall depth is still lacking.

Klopp now has the opportunity to prove that the right manager can make the difference — even if Shearer does not believe Germany is ready to return to the very top just yet.

articles.title: Tiger Top Spin: Six weeks of work begin to pay off for Mizzou tennis
articles.summary: Mizzou Tennis leaves Charlotte with a second consecutive positive record
articles.body:
Mizzou tennis is beginning to see the results of six weeks of work come together on the court. After spending much of the fall building new habits and learning how to compete as a team, the Tigers continued their progress with a strong showing at the 49er Invite in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Mizzou finished the two-day tournament with 12 wins across singles and doubles against players from Charlotte, Clemson, Maryland and Rutgers. The Tigers also recorded their second consecutive tournament with a positive record, giving the team another sign that its work is translating into competition.

The tournament opened Thursday evening with four single-set doubles matches, and Mizzou won all four. Freshmen Irina Anghel and Danielle Chapman defeated Clemson's Neilson-Gatenby and Sophie Clayton 6-0, while Daria Budko and Mariana Higuita Barraza earned a 6-4 victory against Maryland's Mila Mulready and Anastasiia Sorska.

The Tigers carried that momentum into Friday, adding two doubles victories and two singles wins during the first round. Chapman and Budko each earned their first collegiate singles victories against Rutgers opponents, giving both players another milestone during the fall season.

Mizzou saved another strong stretch for the final round, winning six consecutive matches to close the tournament. Chapman earned her second singles victory of the weekend in straight sets against Charlotte, while Budko battled through three sets for her second win of the invite, and Anghel and Higuita Barraza each earned their first singles victories.

For associate head coach Manny Raga, who traveled with the team to Charlotte, the results were a reflection of the work the players have put in since the start of the fall.

"We are building in the right direction," Raga said. "All the hard work they have been putting into their tennis the last six weeks is paying off."

Raga also pointed to the way the players represented Mizzou throughout the tournament, emphasizing their competitiveness and discipline. Those qualities have become an important part of the team's development as the Tigers continue learning how to rely on one another during competition.

"Really proud to see the girls representing Mizzou the right way," Raga said. "Competing hard for every point, playing disciplined and smart tennis."

Head coach Robin Goodman has noticed the same growth as Mizzou has put together positive results in consecutive tournaments. The wins matter, but Goodman said the larger development has been seeing the players learn how to compete for each other and maintain their effort throughout every point.

"Great tournament again for us," Goodman said. "Two tournaments back to back where we've left with a positive record. The girls are learning how to compete as a team and give all they have for every point."

The 49er Invite provided another checkpoint for a team that is still developing its identity, with several players earning first collegiate victories and the Tigers consistently finding ways to finish matches. After six weeks of preparation, the progress is beginning to become visible when Mizzou faces outside competition.

The Tigers will have another opportunity to measure that progress at the ITA Central Regional in Memphis, Tennessee, from Oct. 14-19. With nearly two weeks before the next competition, Mizzou can use the time to continue building on the habits that have helped produce two positive tournaments and carry that momentum into the next stage of its fall season.

Columns and Courts will be back Wednesday with more insight into Mizzou tennis. Tigers Top Spin will be back next Monday.

articles.title: Snap counts: Back-7 still searching for answers vs. Panthers
articles.summary: Exploring the Detroit Lions snap counts from Week 4 vs. Carolina Panthers.
articles.body:
The Detroit Lions suffered yet another disappointing loss on national television, their second of the season, this time falling to the Carolina Panthers 32-26 on "Sunday Night Football." Let's look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward.

Goff threw for 412 yards in this game, but like several other players on this roster, came up short in some critical moments. In a game where the defense was so bad that he needed to be near perfect to keep the Lions competitive, this time he came up just a bit short.

Sione Vaki: 12 (17%) — 18 special teams snaps (60%)

With the Lions trailing most of the game and by double digits in the second half, the Lions tried to keep Gibbs on the field as much as possible, and he saw an uptick in his usage—even though his production resulted in the lowest output of the season.

The switch flipped for Williams in this game, and he showed signs of the player we saw in training camp, giving some hope that in future games he can help open things up for the offense. St. Brown's eight receptions on 11 targets might be the quietest productive game of his career. TeSlaa remains a situational big-play threat, while the reserves are simply special teamers.

With the Lions trailing, we saw more 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) in this game, and as a result, a big dip in the tight ends' reserve snap counts. Wright saw his snaps scaled back around 40%, while Meeks didn't see the field on offense at all.

LG Christian Mahogany: 71 (100%) — 6 (20%)

Only two Jumbo (6th OL) sets in this game, which isn't overly surprising considering one of the two snaps was completely ineffective. The offensive line as a whole was solid in pass protection, sporadic in run blocking, and took far too many penalties—six for the group—especially in critical moments.

3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 32 (43%) — 6 (20%) — 1 offensive snap (1%)

The Lions defensive line was the bright spot of the defense, and even they took a step back from previous week's production. Panthers quarterback Bryce Young was quick and efficient with his throws, and even in situations where the Lions' interior created push, the ball was out before they could get home. McNeill was arguably the Lions' best defender on Sunday, registering another sack, two quarterback hits, and two tackles for loss.

Rush End Eric O'Neill: 0 (0%) — 19 (63%)

Big End Ahmed Hassanein: DNP ( INACTIVE )

The role opposite Hutchinson remains a rotation between Wonnum and Lacy, and the pair saw a near-even split in this game, unlike previous games where one side got heavy snaps. Fans are still waiting on Moore to see significant playing time, but the second-round rookie has been relatively quiet, save a play where he stunted and pressured Young up the middle.

WILL Malcolm Rodriguez: 28 (37%) — 9 (30%)

WILL Amen Ogbongbemiga: 0 (0%) — 24 (80%)

The third linebacker role was once again a rotation of Rodriguez—who has started the last two games—and Nowaske—who has outsnapped Rodriguez both times. Rookie Rolder is still getting his feet wet after returning from a training camp hamstring injury, but he registered three tackles on the day. This group has been stretched thin with the defensive line pass rushing and the secondary struggling; they're starting to make mistakes, looking overwhelmed, trying to do too much, or hesitating.

NB/CB Roger McCreary: 75 (100%) — 6 (20%)

CB Rock Ya-Sin: 0 (0%) — 9 (30%) — injured during game

The Lions stuck with their starters from last game—in both base and subpackages—and the results were disastrously the same… the problem is: I'm not sure there's a better option right now. Barring a trade, or some drastic improvements in their fundamentals—both in man and zone coverages—this unit is going to cripple the Lions' chances of winning on a weekly basis.

NB/S Christian Izien: 73 (97%) — 6 (20%)

After a terrific Week 3 performance, Izien came back to earth against the Panthers, as both he and Clark looked vulnerable in coverage and saw their weaknesses exposed. The return of Brian Branch would certainly go a long way to stabilizing this unit, but the safeties group has dealt with far too many injuries, is being asked to cover the corners' mistakes, and, in turn, is making mistakes of their own.

articles.title: 5 key plays from Cowboys win over the Texans
articles.summary: What was your favorite play from Sunday’s win?
articles.body:
Another week, another harrowing finish for the Dallas Cowboys. They needed this one desperately to avoid a 1-3 start, and through the heroics of CeeDee Lamb and Dak Prescott, they hung on in a 34-30 thriller.

Even better, the Los Angeles Rams did them a favor by beating the Philadelphia Eagles, so it was a good day as the Cowboys won and it wasn't so sunny in Philadelphia. The clutch victory came down to several pivotal moments. Here are the five key plays that delivered the much-needed win.

Lamb's 30-yard pickup jump-starts the second-half offensive flurry

Down 16-6 at the break, the Cowboys had themselves largely to blame. A blocked 62-yard field-goal attempt late in the second quarter gave Houston a chance to tack on three more points, and the Texans took a 10-point lead into intermission.

For most of the first half, Dallas' offense couldn't do anything right against Houston's pass rush. The tide turned on the opening possession of the third quarter.

After a pair of successful runs, the Cowboys dialed up play-action. Prescott sold the fake, stepped up to elude Will Anderson and the edge pressure, and found an open Lamb in a soft spot in the middle of the defense for 30 yards. That connection put Dallas deep in the red zone.

On the next snap, Javonte Williams scored the first of his three touchdowns behind strong offensive-line blocking. The play ignited an offense that stayed on fire the rest of the afternoon.

There are few things George Pickens does better than catching contested balls and drawing flags. After hauling in a spectacular 53-yard grab over Kamari Lassiter, Pickens kept working. On third-and-7 deep in the red zone, Lassiter was flagged for defensive pass interference as Pickens worked off the line, giving the Cowboys a fresh set of downs at the one.

Lassiter looked stunned, as did many of the Houston fans. Three plays later, on fourth-and-goal, Lassiter grabbed Pickens' jersey for a holding penalty that kept the drive alive. Williams punched it in on the next play to cut the deficit to three.

Without those two flags, Dallas likely would have failed to score on the possession. Given how the Cowboys' defense has performed this season, Houston could easily have answered with a long drive to widen the gap even further. Lassiter's inability to play clean football proved costly.

Christian Parker's tenure as defensive coordinator has drawn plenty of criticism, even with the unit depleted by injuries. Communication breakdowns and coverage issues have been recurring problems, especially in zone.

After the Cowboys closed the gap to 23-20, Parker needed a stop. Facing third-and-8 from their own 42, Houston was one conversion away from field-goal range for Ka'imi Fairbairn.

Parker sent pressure that overloaded the middle and brought Dee Winters off the edge. The blitz was in C.J. Stroud's face immediately; the quarterback had just enough time to scramble and throw the ball away. Dallas capitalized on the ensuing possession to take its first lead of the game.

The comeback nearly died before it fully arrived. On the game-winning drive, Prescott went looking for Lamb in a tight window. Jalen Pitre broke on the throw and had a real chance at the interception, but the ball slipped through his hands.

Had Pitre secured it, the Cowboys would have faced roughly 2:10 remaining and needed a defensive stop after already burning a timeout on a failed challenge earlier. Instead, the drive stayed alive, and Dallas eventually took the lead for good.

Houston's 13 penalties created multiple self-inflicted wounds, but none will haunt them more than the one that got away.

Of course the game-winner has to close the list. Time and again, Dallas found Lamb in favorable matchups against the Texans secondary. With the game on the line, they went back to the well one more time.

Isolated in the slot against Pitre, Lamb got separation. Prescott, with solid protection, scanned the field and delivered a strike into the end zone. The 12-yard touchdown with 40 seconds left gave Lamb his 17th catch of the day, a career high and the second-most receptions in a single game in franchise history.

Dallas held on through Stroud's final Hail Mary attempt to improve to 2-2. Lamb's performance felt like something out of a movie, and the final catch delivered the Hollywood ending the Cowboys desperately needed.

articles.title: Former LPGA No. 1 becomes first to complete career grand slam in Japan
articles.summary: A 30th victory on the JLPGA also gives her a lifetime exemption on that tour.
articles.body:
The reaction said it all. Jiyai Shin dropped her putter, arched her back and covered her face with her hands in a moment of sweet relief. A playoff victory at the Japan Women's Open made her the first player in JLPGA history to win all four majors.

A 30th tour victory on the JLPGA also gives her a lifetime exemption on that tour. According to Korea JoongAng Daily , she's the seventh player to earn the exemption. Shin defeated Japan's current top player, Shiho Kuwaki, with a birdie on the third playoff hole in rainy conditions.

"I kept you waiting," Shin posted on Instagram . "I finally did it. Thank you."

Shin's dominance as a player goes all the way back to 2007, when she played in 19 events on the KLPGA and won 10 of them. The next year, she won her first major, the Women's British Open by three strokes over Yani Tseng to earn LPGA status. Shin won 11 times on the LPGA, including a second British Open, and rose to No. 1 in the world before opting to move closer to home to compete on the JLPGA.

Shin won her first major on the JLPGA in 2015 and now owns six on that tour. She has twice won the Korea Women's Open and is a 21-time winner on the KLPGA. With nearly 70 titles worldwide, Shin still competes in several LPGA majors each season and contends.

She took a share of second at the 2023 U.S. Women's Open at Pebble Beach and posted top-3 finishes at the Women's British in 2023 (3rd) and 2024 (T-2).

articles.title: Fantasy Football Stock Report: Malik Nabers shows up for managers while Josh Downs disappears in Week 4
articles.summary: After a wild Week 4, Matt Okada takes you through which players are on the up and others who are trending down for fantasy football.
articles.body:
As I write this on Sunday night, 15 of 16 Week 4 games are in the books (with Monday night remaining) and the season is continuing to round into shape. Sort of. There were promising improvements. Concerning trends. Performances that changed our early outlook on players and teams. As always, some of these shifting perspectives will have permanent ramifications in fantasy.

With that in mind, I've compiled another full fantasy stock report. These are the most notable risers and fallers heading into Week 5.

After a decent Week 1 with Jaxson Dart at quarterback, Malik Nabers disappeared the next two weeks with (mostly) Jameis Winston. Nabers was banged up throughout and totaled six catches for 27 yards in Weeks 2 and 3 ... before exploding back into relevance this Sunday.

Nabers caught six of his seven targets against the Cardinals and took them for 112 yards, including a 39-yarder on the Giants' first drive and a 25-yard touchdown before halftime. And while Isaiah Likely did see a monstrous 12 targets, no other wide receiver in New York had more than three . It was a good first step to reestablishing Nabers where he belongs: comfortably atop the New York passing game pecking order.

The hope, moving forward, is that Winston and Nabers have finally established some chemistry after the former was forced into action in Week 2. If true, Winston has always been a fantasy-friendly quarterback and Nabers could find his way back into WR1 territory the rest of the way. Oh, and next week brings a matchup with the Washington Commanders — you might want to trade for Nabers just to play him in that game.

Speaking of highly-touted receivers struggling through bad QB play before breaking out in Week 4 ... how about fourth overall pick Carnell Tate?! The Titans rookie was quiet through his first three games, logging single-digit fantasy points in each outing, but did catch six of nine targets in a rainy Week 3 against the Giants. Then, on Sunday, Tate snagged nine of a whopping 12 targets and racked up 145 receiving yards in a close loss to the Ravens.

While QB Cam Ward still didn't look exceptional — and frankly might be one of the least effective starters in the league — it appears he and Tate are getting on the same page. If we exclude Travis Hunter — who was only partially a wideout and missed half his rookie season — the last four rookie wide receivers drafted top-four overall all scored between 165 and 185 half-PPR fantasy points. That's comfortable WR2 range ... and it looks like Tate might now be on his way to joining the list.

Even with his Week 3 receiving touchdown, DK Metcalf had been incredibly disappointing as the "WR1" in Pittsburgh through three weeks, falling short of five catches and 50 receiving yards in all three outings. He was beginning to look like a completely untrustworthy FLEX-play-at-best ... before smoking the Browns for 115 yards on five catches on Thursday Night Football. And while I'm not ready to crown Metcalf as a rest-of-season fantasy WR2 just yet, there are underlying reasons for optimism.

Metcalf and Aaron Rodgers had been mismatched and inefficient for most of the season, but the wideout has now seen 9+ targets in three of four games. Additionally, the entire offense has been adjusting to Mike McCarthy as play-caller and Brian Angelichio as OC after years of Arthur Smith, so it's entirely possible it continues to gel as the season progresses. Metcalf still needs to show some consistency — and ideally get his catch rate over 50% — before we can start him reliably, but TNF was a big step in the right direction.

Wow. After the entirety of the NFL media-sphere spent the week trying to solve the mystery of "What's wrong with Drake Maye?" ... Maye answered himself, with 269 passing yards, 54 rushing yards, three touchdown passes and a 29-26 win over the Bills. He scored 27.16 fantasy points on Sunday, more than he'd scored in the three prior weeks combined (21.6). And he did it in a game Mack Hollins exited early, thanks to a breakout fantasy day from Romeo Doubs.

The former Packers wide receiver finally did what he used to do best in Green Bay and caught two of Maye's three TD tosses (with the third going to Efton Chism III on an absurd one-handed snag). Doubs is averaging 12.8 points per game over the past three weeks, and if Maye and the offense are fixed, Doubs could be a valuable top-30 WR moving forward.

Additionally, A.J. Brown should be back shortly, which would theoretically provide a massive boost for Maye and the offense as a whole, arguably forming a "rising tide lifts all ships" phenomenon in New England. Hopefully you didn't drop Maye, and hopefully the improvement continues deeper into October. Both these players should be rostered with hope on the horizon.

In what might have been one of the more baffling performances of the week, Kyle Monangai handled 30 of the 49 running back carries for Chicago in Sunday's win over the Jets. Not only that, but he racked up 146 rushing yards and two touchdowns on those carries, vastly outproducing D'Andre Swift on the ground and finishing with 27.5 fantasy points. Notably, Monangai did come away from the game with a thumb injury, so that will need to be monitored, but you don't typically see performances like this fade into obscurity.

Moreover, this is already Monangai's second game with at least 124 scrimmage yards and a touchdown through four games (also Week 1), and he's somehow the RB12 overall on the season. It's going to be very hard to write this off as a fluke, and might put Monangai in the FLEX consideration on a weekly basis ... at least. In a great matchup with the Packers next Sunday, he'll very nearly be a must-start at the position (if active).

Josh Downs had a near-ideal situation in the London game against Washington. Alec Pierce and Keenan Allen sidelined, leaving Laquon Treadwell and Ashton Dulin as his only competition. He was facing an absurdly soft Commanders defense that had been shredded by wide receivers. Annnnd ... he responded with three catches for 16 yards on just four targets (all fewer than either of the two names mentioned above, as well as tight end Tyler Warren). It was frankly demoralizing after he appeared to be one of the best "Starts" of the week, and it raises serious questions about his upside moving forward.

What's problematic is a good portion of the blame can be placed on quarterback Daniel Jones, who continued to look absolutely awful (55.9% completion rate, 4.2 yards per attempt, no TD, one INT) on Sunday. Jones has averaged just 188.5 passing yards per game and has three touchdown passes in four games, and that kind of quarterback production makes it hard to support one viable pass-catcher, let alone a top tight end and eventually three wide receivers (plus one of the most persistent and voluminous run games in the league). Park Downs back on the bench until he shows us something meaningful and consistent.

Through four weeks, Jalen Hurts has scored progressively fewer fantasy points each and every game. He scorched the Commanders in Week 1, but that has proven to be a somewhat empty scorching given how Washington's defense has played. After that, he threw two picks and had 18.16 fantasy points against Tennessee, then scored fewer than 14 points in back-to-back outings against the Bears and Rams.

The departure of A.J. Brown (and also DeVonta Smith being out this past Sunday) likely isn't helping, but there's a far more concerning trend with Hurts. He has just one rushing touchdown all season and is averaging just 26.3 rushing yards per game. The YPG matches the decline we saw last year, and the one TD suggests his mark of eight in 2025 might now be an optimistic ceiling. After years in which Hurts averaged 40-50 rushing yards per game and rushed for double-digit scores with ease, this is massively affecting both his floor and his ceiling.

For context, he's averaging the fourth-fewest passing yards per game among all qualified quarterbacks (behind Cam Ward and Daniel Jones, among others) and his seven touchdown passes are only enough to get him to QB12 on the season. Barring a major revitalization for Hurts and Philly's offense, it's going to be very tough for him to finish anywhere near the top five or six at the position, where he has typically lived in recent years.

While you can't drop David Montgomery in any reasonably sized league, you simply cannot start him anymore either. After his monster 27.4-point outing in Week 1 against the Bills, Montgomery has scored 3.5, 5.8 and 4.3 fantasy points in the three games since. He has not topped 11 carries or 35 rushing yards in any of those games, has not found the end zone once since scoring thrice in the opener and is consistently losing drives, snaps and touches to Woody Marks (who hasn't been much better, by the way).

Monty's 2.7 yards per carry are second-worst among qualified RBs (ahead of only MarShawn Lloyd) and his 23.4% success rate is dead last . Even with Week 1 boosting his numbers, Montgomery is winning a "race" for least efficient back in the NFL, and thanks to that Week 1 performance, he has now killed fantasy managers three weeks in a row. This past Sunday, the dud came in a game Houston scored 30 points against an extremely soft Cowboys defense. Whatever it was that we saw in Week 1, it currently appears to be a mirage, and Montgomery should not be started until we see some form of tangible improvement.

Fantasy managers who rejoiced after Henderson's 16 carries for 76 yards and a touchdown in his 2026 debut two weeks ago are wringing their hands and losing hair after Sunday. Henderson scored fewer than five fantasy points for the second straight week, this time despite seeing 16 opportunities. He turned those opportunities into just 42 total yards, was outproduced by Rhamondre Stevenson as a receiver (again) and even lost a goal-line touchdown to Stevenson as well.

Simply put, this backfield cannot be trusted. Even with the New England offense finding its spark ( see Drake Maye and Romeo Doubs above ), it's clear they want to use Stevenson and Henderson in an unpredictable, heavily mixed-and-matched manner — one which will typically favor Stevenson where it matters most for fantasy (in the passing game and the red zone).

Will Henderson have another huge touchdown run (or two or three) this season? Almost certainly. Will we be able to predict when it's coming? Almost certainly not. You might be able to play him in games the Patriots are heavily favored to win, against very soft run defenses, but even that will be dicey. Ultimately, you're probably best served keeping him on your bench and hoping something shifts in the pecking order.

articles.title: What happened between Ireland and Israel in their Nations League match?
articles.summary: Spitting allegations, no handshakes, and bowed heads headlined the second Nations League fixture.
articles.body:
Tensions between the football teams of Israel and Ireland reached a flashpoint during the second leg of their Nations League fixture in Serbia, bringing an end to a politically charged two weeks.

The League 3 Group B match ended in a 1–1 draw at the TSC Arena in Backa Topola on Sunday, but tempers flared and accusations flew despite the game being held behind closed doors and at a neutral venue.

It built on the confrontational nature of their first match on September 27, when Ireland defeated Israel 3-0 .

Irish players had been under pressure from home – where affinity with Palestinians is strong – to boycott the second match against Israel, although the pressure seemed greater during the first game.

“I felt that pressure growing day by day and it’s getting almost to a breaking limit now,” Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said at the time.

Here’s a look at the events surrounding the fixture:

What are the spitting allegations against Israel?

Irish media reported that one of Ireland’s coaches, Damien Doyle, had accused an Israeli player of spitting at him after the half-time whistle.

“I was there. I’m not going to comment. It’s something a disciplinary committee will look at,” Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said when asked by reporters about the incident.

Israel coach Ran Ben-Shimon said he had already left the sideline and did not see what happened.

“Half-time, I was in the dressing room, in my room with my ⁠⁠staff; I didn’t see anything. When I’m going to see and check, I will get ⁠⁠back to you with the answer,” he told reporters.

Will UEFA take action against Israeli players?

There is no clarity yet on whether European football’s governing body will sanction the players.

UEFA and the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) have not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on whether a disciplinary inquiry has been opened into the incident.

While spitting incidents in football are not uncommon, there have been none previously reported between Irish and Israeli players.

Why did Ireland’s players not shake hands with Israelis?

Ahead of the first fixture, Israel was informed in advance by the FAI that Ireland’s players would not shake hands as a form of silent protest and UEFA accepted the arrangement.

It was one of several protest measures unveiled by David Courell, FAI CEO, at the pre-match news conference. He said there would be no exchange of the customary pennant before the game and that Irish players would wear black armbands in honour of all the victims of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, while donating their match fees to charity.

Irish players also bowed their heads while Israel’s national anthem was being played.

Ireland is one of Europe’s most outspoken critics of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and the FAI chose to stage Sunday’s match behind closed doors in Serbia amid the pressure to withdraw from the fixtures.

Will Ireland and Israel face each other again?

No, Sunday’s match was the second and final fixture between the two sides in the group stage. They will not face each other again in the current Nations League cycle.

“I’m absolutely delighted this is finished,” Hallgrimsson said after Sunday’s match, according to Ireland’s national broadcaster RTE.

When asked whether Ireland and Israel should be drawn in the same group at such tournaments, he said: “No, we shouldn’t.”

“But that’s not for us to decide. It’s UEFA that decides that.”

The Icelandic coach went on to talk about the toll it took on his players.

“I wouldn’t wish for any national team to go through what we have gone through these two weeks. So maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something.”

Hallgrimsson underscored the Irish support for Palestine , saying emotions ran high due to the sentiment.

“There’s obviously a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There’s not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.”

Does UEFA separate teams due to political reasons?

Yes, while UEFA uses a computer-generated system to sort the 54 nations into four pots to create groups, it has certain draw conditions in place to keep certain teams apart due to geopolitical or travel restraints.

The only “prohibited clash” in the 2026-27 cycle was between Bosnia and Herzegovina (League B, pot 2) and Kosovo (League B, pot 4).

Other teams that will not be drawn together due to political reasons based on the UEFA Executive Committee’s decision are:

Why did Ireland’s Finn Azaz not play against Israel?

Ireland player Finn Azaz, whose mother has Israeli heritage, was benched for both fixtures after Hallgrimsson said he “didn’t feel he was ready for the game”.

“Obviously we spoke a lot together and it was just tough on him. I could feel it when I spoke to him,” the Ireland manager told the public broadcaster.

“It tested him more than all of us. So I just felt it was better to leave him out than play him.”

Why were Irish players wearing black armbands?

Ireland players wore black armbands in both fixtures in recognition of Palestinians killed in Gaza.

Israel, meanwhile, wore black armbands featuring “7.10”, a reference to October 7, when armed fighters from Palestinian group Hamas launched attacks in southern Israel , which then launched its genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Have other teams worn armbands at international matches before?

Yes, several teams have worn black armbands to commemorate a player or coach who has passed.

Portugal wore black armbands and observed a moment of silence for midfielder Diogo Jota who was killed in a car crash in July 2025. The team then transitioned to longer-term tributes through custom wristbands bearing the name of Jota and the squad when they competed at the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

All Premier League teams and officials honoured Brazilian legend Pele with black armbands and a minute’s applause prior to kickoffs during certain matches the week of Pele’s death in December 2022.

In 2020, AC Milan and Torino wore black armbands in tribute to NBA legend Kobe Bryant, who supported AC Milan and lived in Italy for several years during his childhood.

articles.title: Medvedev disqualified from China Open for hitting fan with a ball
articles.summary: Russia’s Daniil Medvedev disqualified from China Open for hitting spectator with ball during match with Novak Djokovic.
articles.body:
Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his semifinal against Novak Djokovic at the China Open after he hit a ball into the stands that struck a spectator in the front row on Monday.

The spectator was helped out of the arena, holding a hand over his left eye.

Djokovic was serving for the match at 7-5, 5-3 when Medvedev hit the ball into the stands in apparent frustration.

After a forehand volley winner from Djokovic, the ball bounced off the advertising boards and back towards Medvedev, who smacked a backhand that sailed into the stands.

The spectator who was hit was helped away as Medvedev stood on the court watching.

The chair umpire and tournament supervisor came down onto the court to talk to Medvedev, who didn’t appear to put up much of an argument with the disqualification. Medvedev then walked to the net and shook hands with Djokovic.

The incident was reminiscent of when Djokovic was kicked out of the 2020 US Open for accidentally hitting a line judge in the throat with a ball.

“A bit of a shock, to be honest,” Djokovic said. “I honestly didn’t see what happened. I hope that person is not badly injured. On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil, because I know exactly how he feels to be disqualified in a big match. … I am sure that Daniil didn’t want to do this intentionally. It just happens.”

Medvedev has a history of on-court behaviour issues. He was fined 6,000 euros ($7,000) for unsportsmanlike conduct after he smashed his racket seven times during a 6-0, 6-0 loss to Matteo Berrettini at the Monte Carlo Masters earlier this year.

Djokovic extended his perfect career record at the China Open to 33-0.

Aiming for a seventh China Open title in Tuesday’s final, Djokovic will face ninth-ranked Alex de Minaur, who advanced when Hubert Hurkacz retired due to an apparent injury midway through the second set of their semifinal.

It will be Djokovic’s second final of the year after losing to Carlos Alcaraz at the Australian Open.

With his ranking down to No. 11, this is the first time in eight years that Djokovic is playing a tournament without being in the top 10. It is also his first tournament since a first-round exit from the US Open. The 39-year-old Serb rallied to beat top-seeded Alexander Zverev in the quarterfinals on Sunday.

Against Medvedev, Djokovic was twice caught exceeding the time limit on the serve clock. After first receiving a warning, he was then stripped of his first serve on a crucial break point midway through the second set. But Djokovic still won the point.

Medvedev won only two of 18 break points as the pair of former No. 1s traded one gruelling rally after another.

The match was at the 2-hour, 29-minute mark when Medvedev was defaulted.

“I was three points away from the win,” Djokovic said. “It’s always a big battle with Daniil, and it’s so hard to play him when he’s feeling the ball well in slower conditions with a big serve. But we move on.”

De Minaur led 6-4, 3-2 when Hurkacz — who was barely able to run for balls in the second set — stopped playing.

The nature of Hurkacz’s injury was not immediately clear.

In the third round of the women’s tournament, which ends Sunday, six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek rallied past Donna Vekic 4-6, 7-6 (0), 6-2 and will next meet Iva Jovic, who beat Kamilla Rakhimova 6-1, 7-5.

Elina Svitolina beat Maria Sakkari 6-4, 7-5.

Later, Coco Gauff was playing 16-year-old Chinese wild card Sun Xinran, who recently won the US Open junior title.

US Open champion Elena Rybakina withdrew from the upcoming Wuhan Open due to a foot injury.

On Saturday, Rybakina lost her first match with the No. 1 ranking when she was ousted in Beijing by No. 118 Alina Charaeva of Armenia in the second round.

“I’ll take some time to rest and recover,” Rybakina was quoted as saying by Wuhan Open organisers.

Charaeva extended her breakout run by beating Sonay Kartal 6-4, 6-1 to reach the last 16.

Daniil Medvedev of Russia looks on after being disqualified in Beijing [Achmad Ibrahim/AP]

articles.title: Five Takeaways from Mizzou Women’s Basketball Media Day
articles.summary: Coach Kellie Harper and players preview the 2026/27 season
articles.body:
The calendar has officially flipped to October, and with Mizzou women's basketball's first exhibition game approaching, the Tigers are starting to get a better sense of what this year's team can become.

There are plenty of new faces. Mizzou added five freshmen and three transfers, giving Kellie Harper a less experienced, but potentially more versatile roster for her second season in Columbia. If one theme came through in Harper's media availability, though, it was clear: this team is competitive.

Harper repeatedly praised the Tigers' toughness and willingness to push one another in practice, and the players echoed that message, describing a preseason built around physicality, competition and learning how to play together.

1. This team is already embracing Harper's identity

Harper didn't have to search very hard for the word she wanted to describe this group. "Competitiveness" came up again and again. She said the Tigers have consistently pushed one another in practice and that she has seen a level of toughness she believes is greater than what Mizzou had last season.

The players are seeing the same thing. Nevaeh Caffey, one of Mizzou's three transfers, said the team is trying to bring that competitive edge into every drill.

"Just coming in and bringing it every day, winning the drills, winning against the practice players, and trying to win every drill," she said.

That environment extends beyond simply trying to beat the person across from you. Caffey said the Tigers are close off the court while also pushing each other on it, a dynamic that could be important for a team with so many new pieces.

"We got a lot of new people," Caffey said, "so just trying to figure each other out and see how we can perform together as a team."

For now, Harper likes the direction the group is heading.

2. The freshmen are going to have to grow up quickly

Five freshmen is a lot under any circumstances, and five freshmen in the SEC is an entirely different challenge. Harper made it clear that the young players aren't simply here to learn from the bench. They're going to play meaningful minutes, and the coaching staff knows there will be mistakes along the way.

The freshmen are already getting a firsthand lesson in what that means. Cecilie Brandimore described her first few months in college basketball as a major adjustment, particularly when it comes to the physicality of the SEC. Her first practice was something of a wake-up call.

"We had two girls diving after the basketball, like fully putting their bodies on the floor," Brandimore said.

That was enough to make the difference between high school and college basketball pretty clear.

"It kind of just set my mind of like, oh my gosh, we're here," she said.

Ellie Muller is experiencing a similar transition. The day-to-day demands are different, and she's had to learn how to compete against bigger and stronger players. For Khloe Ford, the biggest adjustment has been mental. She knows she can handle the physical side, but she's learning how to trust herself while competing against some of the best players she's ever faced.

That learning curve will be one of the bigger storylines to watch as the season progresses. Harper, though, isn't expecting perfection. She knows there will be an adjustment period, and the expectation is that the group continues to improve as it gains experience.

3. Mizzou's veterans are going to be critical to that development

The freshmen aren't navigating that transition alone. Harper pointed to her veteran players as people the coaching staff can rely on while the younger Tigers learn the system and adjust to college basketball, and the players are leaning on them, too. Ford specifically mentioned the value of learning from Mizzou's experienced players and said she's comfortable asking them questions when she's unsure about something.

That veteran presence matters even more because the roster is so young. Harper singled out the returning core of Grace Slaughter, Abbey Schreacke and Averi Kroenke as players who understand what it means to be part of the Mizzou program, describing them as trusted leaders who love the school and understand what is expected in the locker room and community.

Kroenke's return is particularly significant after she missed last season with an injury. Harper said she had a strong summer and was back to full participation by the end of it, and described her as a vocal, confident player who can handle the ball and provide size. For a team still learning how to play together, those voices could be valuable both on the court and in the locker room.

4. Mizzou wants to play fast, and the players are buying in

There's also a clear identity beginning to emerge on the offensive end. Brandimore described Mizzou's offense as naturally fast-paced and said the Tigers have been emphasizing quick decisions and getting shots up early in possessions. In practice, the team has even used shortened time constraints to force itself to play faster. The idea is simple: if Mizzou becomes comfortable scoring quickly in practice, the normal shot clock should feel more manageable once games begin.

For a young team, that pace could be useful. Rather than asking five freshmen to slow down and process every decision, Mizzou can emphasize running, spacing and attacking. That doesn't mean there won't be mistakes; there will be plenty. But the Tigers appear comfortable making those mistakes while playing aggressively, which fits Harper's broader message throughout the preseason. She wants them to play with confidence and pressure rather than spending possessions worrying about what could go wrong.

Harper isn't hiding the standard she's setting. Postseason basketball remains the goal, and when asked to be more specific, she said Mizzou wants to make the NCAA Tournament. The Tigers aren't simply trying to duplicate last year's 12-3 start, either. Harper said the focus has to be on getting better throughout nonconference play, from October to November and from November to December, while finding both the wins Mizzou should get and opportunities to beat teams it isn't expected to beat.

That's a particularly important distinction for this roster. There are too many new pieces to know exactly what Mizzou will look like in March, but Harper doesn't seem interested in lowering expectations because of that uncertainty.

The players seem to be embracing that mentality. Mizzou's returning players bring familiarity, the transfers bring experience and toughness, and the freshmen bring athleticism, size and plenty of room to grow. Now the challenge is figuring out how all of those pieces fit together. If media day was any indication, the Tigers are comfortable with that challenge and eager to see what this group can become.
